topics.title: Democracy, Representation and Liberal Democracy
topics.benchmark_preservation: The approved design reference, prior topic artifacts and canonical Political Theory owners remain immutable.

panels.panel_title: Meaning, Stakes and the Classical Democratic Map
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Meaning, Stakes and the Classical Democratic Map
[1] Democracy means rule of the people, but Topic 22 asks how rule is restrained.
v
[2] Gauba moves from Greek participation to modern representative institutions.
v
[3] Elections are necessary to modern democracy, but not sufficient by themselves.
v
[4] Liberal democracy adds consent, accountability, rights and minority security.
v
VERDICT -> Topic 22 treats democracy as restrained people-rule.
ANSWER USE -> Define popular rule, then add restraint and protection.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Direct, Representative and Liberal Democracy
[1] Direct democracy expects citizens to deliberate and decide public affairs.
v
[2] Representative democracy uses elected intermediaries for large modern states.
v
[3] The scale problem explains the shift from assembly to representation.
v
[4] The democratic risk is distance between rulers and the people.
v
VERDICT -> Representation solves scale but creates accountability risk.
ANSWER USE -> Contrast feasibility with democratic distance.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Necessary and Sufficient Democratic Conditions
[1] Liberal democracy joins popular authorisation to constitutional restraint.
v
[2] Its core package is consent, accountability, majority rule and minority rights.
v
[3] Civil liberties, party competition and courts protect the reality of choice.
v
[4] Majority rule is a decision rule, not unrestricted domination.
v
VERDICT -> Liberal democracy joins authorisation to rights and law.
ANSWER USE -> Separate necessary elections from sufficient safeguards.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Classical Critics and Comparative Defenders
[1] Plato fears demagogy, incompetence and instability under unchecked democracy.
v
[2] Aristotle accepts collective judgment but warns against false equality claims.
v
[3] Dicey and Bryce defend democracy through majority opinion and public welfare.
v
[4] Classical criticism and modern defence both belong inside Topic 22 answers.
v
VERDICT -> Classical criticism tests democracy without exhausting it.
ANSWER USE -> Pair each thinker with one precise risk or gain.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Locke, Mill, Rousseau and Dewey
[1] Locke and Bentham defend accountable government against abuse of power.
v
[2] Mill links representation to liberty, criticism and civic improvement.
v
[3] Rousseau insists sovereignty stays with the people and resists alienation.
v
[4] Dewey extends democracy into communication, inquiry and associated living.
v
VERDICT -> Key thinkers differ over sovereignty, liberty and civic life.
ANSWER USE -> Compare what each protects and what each fears.

panels.panel_title: Representation: Territorial, Functional and Normative Models
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Representation: Territorial, Functional and Normative Models
[1] Territorial representation organises constituencies through geography.
v
[2] Functional representation seeks voice for occupations or sectoral interests.
v
[3] Gauba notes functional schemes attracted corporatist or totalitarian uses.
v
[4] Representation theory therefore asks about structure as well as legitimacy.
v
VERDICT -> Representation has structural forms as well as role theories.
ANSWER USE -> Keep territorial-functional distinct from delegate-trustee.

panels.panel_title: Electoral Translation, Minority Protection and Trap Repair
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Electoral Translation, Minority Protection and Trap Repair
[1] Delegate theory stresses constituent control over the representative.
v
[2] Trustee theory stresses the representative's own judgment after election.
v
[3] Mandate theory ties election to authorisation of a public programme.
v
[4] Descriptive and substantive representation ask different democratic questions.
v
VERDICT -> Composition and action are different tests of representation.
ANSWER USE -> Ask who mirrors society, then who serves interests.

panels.panel_title: Revision Spine and Secondary Representation Theory
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Revision Spine and Secondary Representation Theory
[1] FPTP elects the largest vote-getter and is not a 50 per cent plus rule.
v
[2] Majoritarian devices seek broader backing through runoff or transfer methods.
v
[3] List PR aligns seats more closely with vote share and improves inclusion.
v
[4] STV is one proportional method using ranked transfer in multi-member seats.
v
VERDICT -> Electoral systems trade off decisiveness, legitimacy and inclusion.
ANSWER USE -> Do not merge plurality, majoritarian and PR rules.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Electoral Trade-offs and Liberal-Democratic Tensions
[1] Concurrent and consociational devices respond to risks of permanent exclusion.
v
[2] Their promise is minority security; their cost can be delay and bargaining.
v
[3] Indian application here stays conceptual: franchise, rights and review matter.
v
[4] Detailed article law remains with Polity owners, not this theory topic.
v
VERDICT -> Minority protection deepens democracy when domination is checked.
ANSWER USE -> Use Indian illustrations conceptually, not article-heavy.

panels.panel_title: Answer Architecture, Indian Application and Provenance
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Answer Architecture, Indian Application and Provenance
[1] Verified Philosophy PYQs must retain original ownership in their source owners.
v
[2] Topic 22 answers start with threshold: define, then test sufficiency.
v
[3] Topic 23 adds Schumpeter, Dahl and later models as bounded extensions.
v
[4] Topic 23 must not displace Topic 22's liberal-democratic foundation.
v
VERDICT -> Topic 23 extends Topic 22 rather than replacing it.
ANSWER USE -> Use later models as bounded supplemental bridges.
CENTRAL FOCUS
MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair
[1] Repair the trap that elections automatically prove democracy.
v
[2] Repair the trap that majority rule equals minority suppression.
v
[3] Repair the trap that FPTP is itself a majoritarian 50 per cent system.
v
[4] Repair the trap that descriptive and substantive representation are identical.
v
VERDICT -> Close-option errors come from collapsed threshold distinctions.
ANSWER USE -> State the decisive distinction before choosing.
CENTRAL FOCUS
PYQ Ownership and Answer Practice
[1] This topic uses six original Mains prompts for direct package generation.
v
[2] Forms of Government owns liberal-democracy and democracy-challenge PYQs.
v
[3] Ideals owns liberty-equality-democracy, while Sovereignty owns democracy stems
there.
v
[4] Final recall: democracy needs representation, restraint and public judgment
together.
v
VERDICT -> Cross-applied PYQs help only when ownership is preserved.
ANSWER USE -> Borrow the concept, never reroute the primary owner.
